candidates.quote: To see what is in front of one’s nose needs a constant struggle.
candidates.author: George Orwell
candidates.locator: Tribune, 22 March 1946, the penultimate paragraph; reprinted in The Collected Essays, Journalism and Letters, vol. IV, 1968. Verified verbatim in the full text at orwell.ru
candidates.whyThisMonth: The month's blurb in one sentence: the plain fact in front of you is the one it takes daily work to keep looking at.

candidates.quote: God offers to every mind its choice between truth and repose.
candidates.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
candidates.locator: essay XI, the passage on choosing a creed, 1841. Verified verbatim, Gutenberg 2944, where the next sentence begins Take which you please
candidates.whyThisMonth: The price of clear seeing, named in one line: you can be comfortable about a thing or you can be right about it, and seldom both.

candidates.quote: Transparence means experiencing the luminousness of the thing in itself, of things being what they are.
candidates.author: Susan Sontag
candidates.work: Against Interpretation, in Against Interpretation and Other Essays
candidates.locator: section 9; Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1966, first printed in Evergreen Review, December 1964. HEDGE: the sentence is corroborated in two independent quotations, the section number was not checked against the page
candidates.whyThisMonth: A definition of clear sight that asks nothing of the looker except to let the thing be what it is, which is the whole of this month's work.

candidates.quote: Conceptually, we may call truth what we cannot change; metaphorically, it is the ground on which we stand and the sky that stretches above us.
candidates.author: Hannah Arendt
candidates.work: Truth and Politics, in Between Past and Future
candidates.locator: the closing pages; first in The New Yorker, 25 February 1967, then the enlarged Viking edition of 1968, p. 264. HEDGE: the sentence is corroborated in two scholarly quotations, the page was not opened
candidates.whyThisMonth: Truth set out as the floor and the sky rather than as an opinion to be won, which is the steadiest reason anyone has given for wanting it.

candidates.quote: The public must decide whether it wishes to continue on the present road, and it can do so only when in full possession of the facts.
candidates.author: Rachel Carson
candidates.locator: chapter 2, The Obligation to Endure; Houghton Mifflin, 1962. HEDGE: the sentence is corroborated in three independent quotations credited to Carson, the page was not opened
candidates.whyThisMonth: The plainest statement of why a person needs the facts: nobody can choose a road they have not been allowed to see.

candidates.quote: We are learning that a standard of social ethics is not attained by travelling a sequestered byway, but by mixing on the thronged and common road where all must turn out for one another, and at least see the size of one another’s burdens.
candidates.author: Jane Addams
candidates.locator: chapter I, Introduction; Macmillan, 1902. Verified verbatim, Gutenberg 15487
candidates.whyThisMonth: Seeing the size of somebody else's burden is the first honest act of a day, and it cannot be managed from a quiet side road.

candidates.quote: I ask no favors for my sex. I surrender not our claim to equality. All I ask of our brethren is, that they will take their feet from off our necks, and permit us to stand upright on that ground which God designed us to occupy.
candidates.author: Sarah Moore Grimké
candidates.work: Letters on the Equality of the Sexes, and the Condition of Woman
candidates.locator: Letter II, Woman Subject Only to God, to Mary S. Parker, Newburyport, 7th mo. 17, 1837; Isaac Knapp, 1838. Verified in the scanned 1838 text; the printed sentence opens with But and the quotation starts at I
candidates.whyThisMonth: Plain speech with nothing decorative left in it: she asks no favour, states the case, and names exactly what she wants done.

candidates.quote: There is no department of inquiry in which it is not full as easy to miss truth as to find it, even when the materials from which truth is to be drawn are actually present to our senses.
candidates.author: Harriet Martineau
candidates.work: How to Observe: Morals and Manners
candidates.locator: Part I, Requisites for Observation, the Introduction, the opening sentence of the text; Charles Knight, 1838. Verified verbatim, Gutenberg 33944
candidates.whyThisMonth: The first handbook for observing people honestly opens by admitting how easily the eye goes wrong even with the evidence in front of it.

candidates.quote: He that would seriously set upon the search of truth ought in the first place to prepare his mind with a love of it.
candidates.author: John Locke
candidates.locator: Book IV, ch. XIX, Of Enthusiasm, section 1, the chapter added in the fourth edition of 1700. HEDGE: verified through archive.org full text, including Johnson's Dictionary quoting it under Locke; the Gutenberg text of Volume 2 omits the chapter
candidates.whyThisMonth: Before any method comes an affection: Locke says you have to want the truth before you are able to find it, which is the honest order.

candidates.quote: We know truth, not only by the reason, but also by the heart, and it is in this last way that we know first principles; and reason, which has no part in it, tries in vain to impugn them.
candidates.author: Blaise Pascal
candidates.locator: Section IV, Of the Means of Belief, no. 282 in the Brunschvicg numbering Trotter follows. Verified verbatim, Gutenberg 18269, where the text reads We know truth and not We know the truth
candidates.whyThisMonth: A defence of the knowing that arrives before the argument does, written by a man who trusted argument more than most people alive.

candidates.quote: It is a task to come to see the world as it is.
candidates.author: Iris Murdoch
candidates.locator: p. 91, Routledge and Kegan Paul, 1970; on that pagination the essay is The Sovereignty of Good Over Other Concepts. HEDGE: three independent citations give Murdoch 1970 page 91, the page was not opened
candidates.whyThisMonth: Eleven words that turn clear sight from a gift somebody either has or lacks into a job, which is the only version a reader can act on.

candidates.quote: We ought not to be ashamed of appreciating the truth and of acquiring it wherever it comes from, even if it comes from races distant and nations different from us.
candidates.author: Al-Kindi
candidates.locator: the address to al-Mu'tasim; Al-Kindi's Metaphysics, State University of New York Press, 1974, p. 58. HEDGE: the wording is corroborated in independent quotations, including in Butterworth's edition of Averroes, the page was not opened
candidates.whyThisMonth: The founding sentence of Arabic philosophy is a rule for taking the truth from strangers, which is harder to do than it is to admire.

candidates.author: Ibn Khaldun
candidates.work: The Muqaddimah: An Introduction to History
candidates.locator: the Introduction, opening the account of why reports go wrong, the next sentence beginning There are various reasons; Bollingen Series XLIII, Pantheon, 1958, vol. 1. HEDGE: corroborated in quotations credited to Ibn Khaldun, the page was not opened
candidates.whyThisMonth: Six hundred years early, a working note on why the story you were handed is probably a little wrong, and why that is nobody's conspiracy.

candidates.quote: To experience means to know facts just as they are, to know in accordance with facts by completely relinquishing one’s own fabrications.
candidates.author: Nishida Kitarō
candidates.locator: Part I, ch. 1, Pure Experience, the opening sentences of the text; Yale University Press, 1990, p. 3. Verified in the scanned Abe and Ives text; the Japanese original is Zen no kenkyū, 1911
candidates.whyThisMonth: Modern Japanese philosophy opens by asking for exactly what this month asks for: the facts, minus whatever the looker has added to them.

candidates.quote: Every man takes the limits of his own field of vision for the limits of the world.
candidates.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
candidates.locator: the section headed Further Psychological Observations, listed in the contents as Psychological Observations; Swan Sonnenschein. Verified verbatim, Gutenberg 10732, where the next sentence calls it an error of the intellect
candidates.whyThisMonth: The sentence a person most needs before breakfast: what you can see is not the size of the world, only the size of the window you have.

candidates.quote: Freedom is always and exclusively freedom for the one who thinks differently.
candidates.author: Rosa Luxemburg
candidates.locator: the passage that follows Freedom only for the supporters of the government; written in 1918, first published 1922, this translation Workers Age Publishers, 1940. HEDGE: the wording is the standard Wolfe rendering, corroborated in independent quotations; the chapter number and page were not checked
candidates.whyThisMonth: The plainest test of whether a person actually wants the truth: it is the one who disagrees who has to be free to say so.
